63.0.0.en: 1 Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah? this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength? “I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save.” 2 Wherefore art thou red in thine apparel, and thy garments like him that treadeth in the winefat? 3 “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me: for I have trodden them in mine anger, and trampled them in my fury; and their juice was sprinkled upon my garments, and I have stained all my raiment. 4 For the day of vengeance is in mine heart, and the year of my redeemed is come. 5 And I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered that there was none to uphold: therefore mine own arm brought salvation unto me; and my fury, it upheld me. 6 And I have trodden down the people in mine anger, and made them drunk in my fury, and poured out their juice upon the earth.”

63.0.1.en: In the day of the destruction of Jerusalem at the hands of Babylon, the sons of Edom stood gloating, and even played a positive role against Jerusalem by seizing the fugitives to hand them over as captives, and by entering with their spoils to pasture in Jerusalem, and so on... Therefore the psalmist cries out, saying: “Remember, O LORD, the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem; who said, Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof” (Ps 137:7); and as the prophet Obadiah says: “For thy violence against thy brother Jacob shame shall cover thee, and thou shalt be cut off for ever. In the day that thou stoodest on the other side, in the day that the strangers carried away captive his forces, and foreigners entered into his gates, and cast lots upon Jerusalem, even thou wast as one of them” (Obad 1:10-11).

63.0.2.en: Edom (meaning earth, and a lover of shedding blood) points to the enemy of good, the devil. Therefore the Savior appears as one coming from Edom in red garments, in His majesty and greatness; He overcame the enemy and trod him down as in a winepress, to give His people victory and salvation.

63.0.3.en: “Who is this that cometh from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?! this that is glorious in his apparel, travelling in the greatness of his strength?! I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save” [1].

63.0.4.en: The prophet looked upon the Savior as He was lifted up on the Cross, shattering the true Edom and giving victory and splendor to His believers, and so he began to ask Him:

63.0.8.en: What is Thy work? And what is Thy purpose?

63.0.9.en: As to His person, He says: “I that speak in righteousness, mighty to save” [1]. Many speak of righteousness and are skilled in discoursing about it; even some of the religious leaders of that time were able to teach concerning righteousness. But the Savior, our Lord Jesus, is the only One able to speak of righteousness that is “mighty to save,” that is, practical righteousness that grants deliverance from enemies and the enjoyment of eternity. He alone is the Righteous One who knew no sin (2 Cor 5:21), who bore our sins in His body to atone for them by His shed blood, giving us His righteousness as our righteousness. He is unique in His righteousness: on the one hand, He alone is absolutely without blemish, and on the other hand, He is able to justify others. He is the Righteous One in whom the Father is well pleased, and He carries us in Himself that we too may be counted objects of His good pleasure.

63.0.10.en: The Lord Christ speaks of righteousness not with His mouth only, but with His whole being and His life, which He gave by His holy will through His divine love for the sake of our justification, to restore our corrupt nature and give it fellowship in the divine nature (2 Pet 1:4).

63.0.11.en: As to the place, he saw Him coming from “Edom,” which means “earth” or “blood.” It is as though the Lord came to where we had fallen, to Edom, where we returned to our dust, in order to turn our dust into heaven. It was said to us, “for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return” (Gen 3:19); now that our heavenly Savior has come down to our earth that we may be united with Him, we hear the divine voice: “For heaven thou art, and unto heaven shalt thou return.” This is the righteousness of Christ that lifts us as from the dunghill to set us in His heavens.

63.0.12.en: From another side, since we became “Edom” (= blood), lovers of fighting or haters of others, our Christ came to the field of battle to wrest us from the enemy of good, the lover of shedding blood, that our hearts might be enlarged with love and self-giving!

63.1.0.en: As to His work, He says: “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me” [3]. He entered the battle, the battle of the Cross, alone, as He said to His disciples: “and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (Jn 16:32).

63.1.1.en: His apparel is red and His garments like him that treadeth in the winefat [2], since they put a scarlet robe on Him (Mk 15:17) to mock Him. It also indicates that His whole body poured out blood from the wounds that bring healing (Isa 53:5). This self-giving is the secret of a surpassing beauty, which is perceived by one who has experienced the Cross as the power of God unto salvation; therefore it was said, “glorious in his apparel” [1].

63.1.2.en: * He wrought a wonderful dispensation for the suffering body, for it was adorned with sufferings and glorified with divinity, and there is nothing more sweet and beautiful than that.

63.2.0.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus What He did was inspired by His great love and His zeal for His bride, since He wanted to free her from the enemy, the devil, and to give her the enjoyment of the perpetual year of jubilee, or unbroken liberation [4].

63.3.s.en: 2. A hymn about the Lord's lovingkindnesses:

63.3.0.en: 7 I will mention the lovingkindnesses of the LORD, and the praises of the LORD, according to all that the LORD hath bestowed on us, and the great goodness toward the house of Israel, which he hath bestowed on them according to his mercies, and according to the multitude of his lovingkindnesses. 8 For he said, Surely they are my people, children that will not betray: so he was their Saviour. 9 In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them: in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; and he bare them, and carried them all the days of old.

63.3.1.en: The prophet found nothing that the Church, the bride redeemed by blood, could offer in return for God's constant lovingkindnesses, which were revealed in their deepest form on the Cross, except praise to Him.

63.4.0.en: God did not bestow His lovingkindnesses for the sake of some return, but because of His mercies and the multitude of His lovingkindnesses, looking upon us as His people and His sons; He shares with us our affliction and our sufferings. “In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence (the Savior) saved them” [9]. It is a wonderful love!

63.5.0.en: 10 But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he fought against them. 11 Then he remembered the days of old, Moses, and his people, saying, “Where is he that brought them up out of the sea with the shepherd of his flock? where is he that put his holy Spirit in the midst of them, 12 That led them by the right hand of Moses with his glorious arm, dividing the water before them, to make himself an everlasting name, 13 That led them through the deep, as an horse in the wilderness, that they should not stumble? 14 As a beast goeth down into the valley, the Spirit of the LORD caused him to rest.” So didst thou lead thy people, to make thyself a glorious name.

63.5.1.en: If man in his foolishness takes a stand against his Creator and Redeemer, God in His love remembers His former works with them, how He shepherded them through Moses, and how He dwelt in their midst by His Holy Spirit. He divided the waters before them that His name might be glorified in them... God is still the same, in a love that wants to lead His people Himself!

63.5.2.en: Truly He disciplines them for their hostile stand, but He remains waiting for their return. This is what He meant by saying: “But they rebelled, and vexed his holy Spirit: therefore he was turned to be their enemy, and he fought against them. Then he remembered the days of old,” and so on... [10-11].

63.5.3.en: * If we pray and chant the Psalms before Him in pride, in a critical manner, in arrogance, if we perform the service with a scattered mind, He not only does not listen to us but even delivers us to the evil one... He turns to become an adversary who fights us; in other words, He withdraws us from His presence and delivers us to Satan for our discipline, until we cease from blaspheming (1 Tim 1:20).

63.6.0.en: 15 Look down from heaven, and behold from the habitation of thy holiness and of thy glory: where is thy zeal and thy strength, the sounding of thy bowels and of thy mercies toward me? are they restrained? 16 Doubtless thou art our father, though Abraham be ignorant of us, and Israel acknowledge us not: thou, O LORD, art our father, our redeemer; thy name is from everlasting. 17 O LORD, why hast thou made us to err from thy ways, and hardened our heart from thy fear? Return for thy servants' sake, the tribes of thine inheritance. 18 The people of thy holiness have possessed it but a little while: our adversaries have trodden down thy sanctuary. 19 We have been of old as they over whom thou never barest rule; upon whom thy name was not called.

63.7.0.en: When we fall into evil and stand as enemies of God, God remains waiting for our repentance. So we do not justify our faults, but we move His love and His zeal toward us, since He is our Father, who knows us more than Abraham, the father of the believers, and Israel himself [16].

63.7.1.en: “Look down from heaven, and behold from the habitation of thy holiness and of thy glory” [15]. Thus the sinner feels as though he had defiled the earth with his sin and his abomination, and as though God had left the earth to remain in heaven, where His sanctuary and His glory are; therefore he moves God's mercies, asking Him to look down from His pure heavens upon the fallen soul that longs to return to Him and to enjoy His presence.

63.7.2.en: Perhaps this feeling came as a result of what had befallen the temple of the Lord in destruction, for the prophet Ezekiel saw the glory of the Lord leaving the temple and the city of Jerusalem, indeed the whole earth, when he says: “Then the glory of the LORD departed from off the threshold of the house, and stood over the cherubims. And the cherubims lifted up their wings, and mounted up from the earth in my sight” (Ezek 10:18-19).

63.7.3.en: “Where is thy zeal...? and thy mercies toward me are restrained” [15]. Repentance is built on the discovery of the Lord's zeal toward His children and His surpassing, deep love, “the sounding of thy bowels,” and His mercies toward man, whatever his weaknesses. It is also built on man's awareness of his sonship to Him (Deut 32:6; Isa 63:16).

63.8.0.en: “O LORD, why hast thou made us to err from thy ways? and hardened our heart from thy fear? Return for thy servants' sake, the tribes of thine inheritance” [17]. It is clear here that the penitent does not mean to cast blame on God; rather, having at once discovered God's fatherhood, he reproaches Him, because he had expected that His grace would support him. Truly he sinned and persisted in sin, so God gave him over to a reprobate mind and left him to the hardness of his heart (Rom 1:28); now he asks for His grace, that he may not err from the way of the Lord nor remain in hardness of heart. This is what the psalmist meant by saying: “With my whole heart have I sought thee: O let me not wander from thy commandments” (Ps 119:10).

63.8.1.en: When a person comes under discipline he feels bitterness, and so he stands reproaching God by every means: at one time he asks Him not to allow it any longer, leaving him in the corruption of his mind and the hardness of his heart; at another he asks for His mercy for the sake of His blessed saints who intercede for humanity [17]; and finally he asks Him to hasten to help, since the period of discipline has been long. This is what the prophet expressed by saying: “The people of thy holiness have possessed it but a little while: our adversaries have trodden down thy sanctuary. We have been of old as they over whom thou never barest rule; upon whom thy name was not called” [18-19]. They counted the time in which the people possessed the temple, “the sanctuary of the Lord,” to be short, although it amounts to about 400 years from the building of the temple until the captivity; but the period of the captivity (70 years) they counted as exceedingly long because of its bitterness, for they say, “We have been of old...” They became under the captivity like the rest of the nations, as though God were not ruling over them to rescue them from this bitterness, and as though His name had not been called upon them...

63.8.2.en: Having tasted the bitterness of the captivity, they longed for the Lord to reign over them and to call His name upon them, that He might save them.

64.0.s.en: 1. The descent of the Messiah from heaven:

64.0.0.en: 1 Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might quake at thy presence, 2 As when the fire kindleth the stubble, and the fire causeth the waters to boil, to make thy name known to thine adversaries, that the nations may tremble at thy presence! 3 When thou didst terrible things which we looked not for, thou camest down, the mountains quaked at thy presence.

64.0.1.en: “Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might quake at thy presence, as when the fire kindleth the stubble, and the fire causeth the waters to boil, to make thy name known to thine adversaries, that the nations may tremble at thy presence” [1-2].

64.0.2.en: Some interpreters see that the discourse here concerns the Lord Christ when He descends from heaven openly to establish His kingdom on earth for a thousand years, reigning and defeating His opponents and enemies and all the nations, and so on... in contrast to His first coming, which was hidden in the womb of the Virgin, when He does not cry out nor does anyone hear His voice, and so on...

64.0.3.en: I do not want to speak here about the millennial kingdom, since I dealt with it in the interpretation of chapter 19 of the Book of Revelation; what I want to affirm is that the texts of the prophet Isaiah are not understood in a literal way, because our Christ is a spiritual King, who refused to reign materially, counting His divine Incarnation a descent as from heaven to meet us. We were like mountains in the hardness of our life, and so our depths were shaken; He kindled the stubble of evil within us, and made the cold waters within us boil with love, granting us victory over the enemies of His name, not through visible wars but through faith working by love.

64.0.4.en: For deliverance from captivity or afflictions, it is enough for man to ask God to look down from heaven and behold from the habitation of His holiness and His glory (Isa 63:15), although God fills heaven and earth with His divinity... But for our salvation from our sins and our return to the Father's embrace, the matter requires the rending of the heavens and the descent of the Word of God to our earth [1]. As the Lord Christ said of Himself.

64.0.5.en: * “For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me... that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life: and I will raise him up at the last day” (Jn 6:38-40). He came down from heaven to accomplish obedience in place of the fallen Adam in disobedience, offering the will of the Father, which is one with His will. And the will of the Father is the accomplishment of salvation and resurrection by seeing the Son in faith and abiding in Him.

64.0.6.en: * “No man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven” (Jn 3:13).

64.0.7.en: And St. John the Baptist said of Him: “He that cometh from heaven is above all” (Jn 3:31).

64.0.8.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian praises the Word of God who rent the heavens and came down, saying:

64.0.9.en: [Blessed is He who by His Incarnation bought life for our human nature!

64.0.10.en: Blessed is He who sealed our souls and adorned them and betrothed them to Himself as a bride!

64.0.11.en: Blessed is He who made our body a tent for His invisible nature...!

64.0.12.en: Glory to Him who looked upon us, how we accepted to resemble the beasts in our rage and our greed, and came down to us and became one of us, that we might become heavenly...!].

64.0.13.en: The prophet David looked to the divine Incarnation and said: “He bowed the heavens also, and came down” (Ps 18:9).

64.0.14.en: Some see that by saying “Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might quake at thy presence” [1] he means that the people in the midst of their affliction felt as though God had hidden His face from them with a cloud: “The LORD dwelleth in the thick darkness” (2 Chr 6:1); “Thick clouds are a covering to him, that he is not seen” (Job 22:14). It is as though they were crying out that if our sins have hidden Thee behind the clouds, and have veiled from us the perception of the mysteries of Thy purposes, there is none who can set the matter right but Thyself. We cannot ascend to Thee, but Thou canst rend the veil and come down to us. It is not enough that Thou lookest upon us from Thy heavens; we need Thy dwelling in our midst.

64.0.15.en: “The mountains quake” [1]. If the solid mountains trembled at Sinai when God met with Moses (Ex 19:17-18), and the mountains were rent and the rocks broken in pieces before the Lord when He spoke to Elijah (1 Kgs 19:11), who can stand before Him?! God alone is able to solve all our problems, shaking our old man and shattering the might of our evil in order to establish His kingdom within us. If the devil and all his soldiers and angels, with their evil works and deceits, are like mountains, then the Lord shakes their kingdom by the Cross; and if they are like stubble (like brittle dry straw that is good for nothing but fuel), then God destroys them with fire.

64.0.16.en: We need the Lord to come down to us because our enemies who are like mountains are the enemies of His name; they oppose us to tear us away from His Kingdom or to tear His name and His Kingdom out of us.

64.1.0.en: The opposition of the enemies, the devil and his soldiers, however violent it may be, becomes like stubble that God burns with fire, not only to scatter the opposition but to turn it to good, since He uses these fires to heat the cold waters of our hearts so that they boil with love and holy zeal [2]. St. John Chrysostom says: [Even the devil can be a cause of benefit to us if we understand him... This is clear in the case of Job. We can also learn this from Paul, who writes concerning the fornicator: “To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved” (1 Cor 5:5). See how even Satan has become a cause of salvation, not by his nature, but by the skill of the Apostle, like a physician who takes a viper to extract a medicine from it].

64.2.s.en: 2. The blessings of waiting for the Messiah:

64.2.0.en: 4 For from eternity they have not heard nor given ear, neither hath the eye seen a God beside thee, which worketh for him that waiteth for him. 5 Thou meetest him that rejoiceth and worketh righteousness, those that remember thee in thy ways. Behold, thou art wroth; for we have sinned: it is for ever, and we shall be saved.

64.2.1.en: As the prophets lived awaiting the coming of the Messiah for salvation, we remain always waiting for Him to reign, not on earth, but in our hearts, over our inner life, that He may carry us into the fellowship of His glory; we see what God has prepared for us, and we are filled with joy by His righteousness working in us. The prophet says: “For from eternity they have not heard nor given ear, neither hath the eye seen a God beside thee, which worketh for him that waiteth for him. Thou meetest him that rejoiceth and worketh righteousness...” [4-5].

64.2.2.en: Though God's works have been wonderful from of old, nothing has ever been heard or seen like what the Lord did with mankind through His saving works; for He went forth as from heaven to meet sinners with joy, working righteousness in their lives, granting them inner glories as a pledge of the eternal glory.

64.2.3.en: St. Hippolytus comments on this prophetic statement, speaking in the person of the Lord Christ: [Enter into the Kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. Enjoy forever what is given to you by My Father who is in the heavens and the life-giving Holy Spirit. What mouth can tell of these blessings which eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither have entered into the heart of man, the things which God hath prepared for them that love him (Isa 64:4; 1 Cor 2:9)? You have heard of the unbroken joy! You have heard of the unchanging Kingdom! You have now learned of the banquet of blessings that has no end!].

64.3.0.en: 6 But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away. 7 And there is none that calleth upon thy name, that stirreth up himself to take hold of thee: for thou hast hid thy face from us, and hast consumed us, because of our iniquities. 8 But now, O LORD, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand. 9 Be not wroth very sore, O LORD, neither remember iniquity for ever: behold, see, we beseech thee, we are all thy people. 10 Thy holy cities are a wilderness, Zion is a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation. 11 Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire: and all our pleasant things are laid waste. 12 Wilt thou refrain thyself for these things, O LORD? wilt thou hold thy peace, and afflict us very sore?

64.3.1.en: Our souls remain always rejoicing for God's surpassing saving works, always awaiting a continual meeting with Him, that He may remove the shame of our sins and declare the glory of His righteousness in us. The way of this meeting is:

64.3.2.en: a. Confession of sins: “Behold, thou art wroth; for we have sinned” [5]. St. Cyprian says: [Good is repentance! If it has no place in your heart, you will lose the grace of the washing that you received in Baptism long ago, for it is better for us to have a garment to mend than to have no garment to wear; but once the garment has been prepared for us, it must be renewed...]. And St. John Climacus says: [Repentance renews Baptism, a covenant made with God for a second life]. And St. John Chrysostom says: [Have you sinned? Say to God: “I have sinned.” What toil is there in this...?].

64.3.3.en: b. Our realization of the inability of self-righteousness to save us: “But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags; and we all do fade as a leaf; and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away” [6]. As Father Martyrius the Syrian Martyrius: Sahdona of Halmon says: [Our whole inner being is swallowed up when we see Him (Dan 10:8); because of His majesty our mouths fall silent. When we receive a little strength to speak with Him, our consciences blame us, and we see that we have sinned and done iniquity in His presence (Ps 106:6). If we imagine that we have come to the place of the righteous, all our righteousness is as a menstrual rag (Ex 36:17); to Him belongs victory, but to us confusion of face and shame (Bar 1:15)].

64.3.4.en: Father Theonas shows us how our good works turn to wickedness if we rely on our own righteousness, for our righteousness is counted as a menstrual rag when compared with the divine righteousness.

64.4.0.en: c. Awareness of God's tender fatherhood, which forgives sins: “But now, O LORD, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand. Be not wroth very sore...” [8-9].

64.4.1.en: God presents Himself to us as Father, Bridegroom, Friend and self-giving Shepherd... in order to draw every soul to Himself by repentance. And His Church bears the same mark so as to embrace all with love, that they may enjoy God's wonderful salvation. In a letter to a fallen monk, St. Basil the Great says:

64.4.2.en: [I grieve for you, for what priest does not weep when he hears this...?!

64.4.3.en: What minister of the altar does not beat his breast?!

64.4.4.en: What “layman” is not broken in heart?!

64.4.6.en: You have shattered all at once, all at once you have despised everyone...

64.4.7.en: Remember the good Shepherd who follows you and calls to you...

64.4.8.en: I beg you not to hesitate to come to me because of any earthly consideration, for I lament when I find my dead one, I stay by him and weep for him because of “the spoiling of the daughter of my people” (Isa 22:4).

64.4.9.en: Behold, all are ready to welcome you! All join with you in your striving, so do not draw back...

64.4.10.en: It is a time for salvation, it is a season for amendment!

64.4.11.en: Be cheerful and do not despair, for she (the Church) is not a law that condemns the sinner without mercy, but (she has) a law of mercy that removes the penalty and awaits amendment.

64.4.12.en: Behold, the doors have not yet been shut, the Bridegroom hears...

64.4.13.en: Have pity on yourself and on all of us in our Lord Jesus Christ].

64.5.0.en: d. It reminds us that we are His people who belong to Him [9].

64.5.1.en: e. Our confession of the ruin that has befallen us: we have become a barren wilderness, fires have been kindled within us, and all the inner sanctuaries have been disfigured.
